extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (graduate students and early-career researchers) preparing papers, talks, theses, grants, letters, and other professional writing
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, genre-spanning guidance for writing mathematics (papers, talks, theses, referee reports, letters, grant proposals, etc.), emphasizing clarity, notation discipline, revision, and reader-centered exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying your audience
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Picture a specific reader and write for them; tailor level of detail, motivation, and notation to that imagined reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlining and the role of the table of contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlining; the role of the table of contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an outline and a well-planned table of contents to organize material and guide both writer and reader; think top-down before filling details.

rubrics_metrics.name: First draft and revision cycle
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a first draft, then revise repeatedly — Krantz stresses revise, revise again, then once more; never publish a draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful use of words
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose precise vocabulary; avoid vague qualifiers and tired adjectives that add no information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption of language ('nice', 'interesting', 'very', 'essentially')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid these hollow modifiers; replace with specific, informative descriptions of what is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in writing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be exact about statements, hypotheses, quantifiers, and logical dependence; imprecise language leads to confusion or error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular vs. plural
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep number agreement clear to avoid ambiguity in statements and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronouns and antecedents
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure pronouns have clear antecedents; ambiguous 'it', 'this', 'they' weaken exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acronyms — define on first use; never coin gratuitously
rubrics_metrics.description: Acronyms — define on first use; never coin gratuitously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce acronyms only when they save effort and will be used repeatedly; always expand at first occurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jargon — distinguish technical terms from in-group slang
rubrics_metrics.description: Jargon — distinguish technical terms from in-group slang.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established technical terminology when needed, but avoid insider slang that will confuse readers outside a small circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mnemonic choice of letters
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose variable and function names that suggest their role (e.g., use 'n' for integers, 'x' for variables) to aid reader understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation consistency throughout the paper
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep notation uniform across sections; inconsistent notation forces readers to re-translate and increases error risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't reuse a symbol; avoid double-using letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't reuse a symbol; don't double-use a letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reassigning the same symbol to different objects in the same paper or nearby context; reserve letters for consistent meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscript and superscript discipline
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subscripts/superscripts systematically and sparingly to prevent overly complicated expressions and indexing confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active voice preferred
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor active constructions to make sentences clearer and more direct; passive voice can obscure the actor and reduce clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid filler phrases ('we will see', 'as we shall see')
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the 'we will see' / 'as we shall see' filler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut such anticipatory fillers; state the result or guide the reader with substantive transitions instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph = one idea
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure paragraphs so each develops a single idea; use topic sentences and logical progression within and between paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic sentence first
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin paragraphs with a clear topic sentence that frames what follows; helps readers orient and skim effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-verb agreement
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain correct grammatical agreement to avoid ambiguity and preserve professional tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma overuse and underuse
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use commas to clarify clause boundaries and lists; both overuse and omission can impede comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel construction
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parallel grammatical structures in lists and comparisons to improve readability and rhetorical balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictive vs. non-restrictive clauses
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use punctuation (commas) correctly to signal whether a clause is essential to meaning or parenthetical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem environments and labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem environments: theorem, lemma, proposition, corollary, definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate environment/label for each result; proper labeling helps readers gauge importance and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to display vs. inline a formula
rubrics_metrics.description: When to display vs. inline a formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display long or important formulas for readability; keep short, simple expressions inline to preserve flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation of displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat displayed formulas as part of sentences—punctuate accordingly to maintain grammatical and logical coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbering schemes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a consistent numbering system for equations, theorems, figures, etc., that supports easy cross-referencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofreading: read aloud; read backwards; have a colleague read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple strategies: reading aloud to catch awkward phrasing, reading sections backwards to focus on form, and using peer readers to find errors and unclear passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the copyeditor
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize what a professional copyeditor can fix (surface issues) versus what the author must ensure (mathematical content and logical clarity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Why TeX
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use TeX for professional-quality typesetting of mathematics; it improves readability and consistency across documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common TeX errors that propagate to readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Common TeX errors that propagate to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sloppy TeX (mismatched delimiters, poor spacing, incorrect macros) because such errors confuse readers and may introduce mistakes in displayed mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research paper (genre guidance)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Krantz provides dedicated guidance for writing research papers (organization, motivation, definitions, theorem statements, proofs), though specific chapter details should be consulted in the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey article (genre guidance)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Krantz treats surveys as a distinct genre with their own expectations for breadth, exposition, and references; see chapter for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion piece (genre guidance)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinion pieces require a rhetorical stance and clarity about audience and purpose; Krantz discusses register and evidence appropriate to such pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book review (genre guidance)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book reviews should summarize main themes, assess contributions and readability, and place the book in context; Krantz discusses tone and balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee report (genre guidance)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good report is short, specific, and constructive: begin with a summary of the paper as you understand it, then list errors, then list suggestions, and end with a recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter of recommendation (genre guidance)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Krantz explains the rhetoric of recommendation letters: what hiring committees actually parse, meaning of standard phrases, and the danger of 'damning with faint praise'; be explicit and candid within professional bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant proposal (genre guidance)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first paragraph must answer: what problem, why important, why now, why you, what success looks like. Remove buzzwords and state concrete aims and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: CV / job application (genre guidance)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Krantz provides advice tailored to academic CVs and job materials; focus on clear presentation of qualifications and evidence relevant to the position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk / colloquium (genre guidance)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare exposition appropriate to the audience level, motivate results early, and structure the talk so listeners take away main ideas; see chapter for practical tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis (genre guidance)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Krantz discusses thesis structure, levels of exposition, dissertation conventions, and how to present results and background material effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Email (genre guidance)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat professional email as a genre: be concise, polite, explicit about requests and context, and format for easy reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing a journal
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a journal whose scope, audience, and standards match your paper; consider prestige, speed, likelihood of acceptance, and intended readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with referees
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond constructively to referee reports, address comments specifically, and use polite, evidence-based rebuttals when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galley proofs and indices
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully check galley proofs for typographical and presentation errors; ensure indices and cross-references are accurate before final publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and negotiate copyright transfers and author rights; retain the ability to post preprints when possible and follow publisher policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: The reader is your guest, not your adversary
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader is your guest, not your adversary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a hospitable tone: make it as easy as possible for the reader to follow your ideas rather than presenting obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for a specific reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Write for a specific reader. Picture them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form an internal model of the intended reader's background and expectations, and shape exposition and level of detail accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut everything that does not serve the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut everything that does not serve the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be ruthless in removing tangents, redundant exposition, and gratuitous material that distracts from the main narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words before symbols
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce ideas informally in words before presenting symbolic definitions or formulas so readers understand motivation and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate every definition
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why a definition is introduced and what problems or examples it addresses to help the reader grasp its significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: State every theorem in full before proving it
rubrics_metrics.description: State every theorem in full before you prove it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the statement complete and readable on its own; avoid proving partial or implicit statements that confuse the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples first, then abstraction
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present concrete examples to build intuition before introducing abstract generalizations or formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the present tense for permanent mathematical content
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the present tense for permanent mathematical content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write that a theorem 'states' or 'is' true (present) rather than 'was' true (past) to reflect enduring validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'I' and 'one'; use 'we' sparingly
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer neutral constructions and be mindful of voice; use 'we' only when it genuinely represents a collaborative or guiding stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite generously; plagiarize never
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge prior work and influences thoroughly; attribute ideas and results to avoid ethical and scholarly violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge contributions from colleagues, students, referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge contributions from colleagues, students, referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give credit in acknowledgments for helpful discussions, corrections, and feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise. Then revise again. Then once more.
rubrics_metrics.description: Revise. Then revise again. Then once more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan multiple revision passes focusing on structure, clarity, and polishing language; iterative refinement is essential to good mathematical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: The first sentence is the most important
rubrics_metrics.description: The first sentence is the most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft opening sentences that hook the reader and clearly state context, problem, or main result.

rubrics_metrics.name: The last sentence is the second most important
rubrics_metrics.description: The last sentence is the second most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclude sections and papers with sentences that summarize impact, connect to broader questions, or provide a clear take-away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never publish a draft
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure work has been adequately revised and proofread before dissemination to preserve reputation and aid readers.
